title: A double portion (2 Kings 2:1–15)
hookLine: Elijah rises in a whirlwind; Elisha picks up his mantle
carry: an old cloak lying on the ground

cards: Everyone seems to know what's about to happen. Elijah and his student Elisha are walking from Gilgal, and Elijah says: stay here, the Lord has sent me to Beth-el.
Elisha answers with an oath: as the Lord lives, I will not leave thee. At Beth-el, prophets come out and ask Elisha, do you know the Lord will take your master today? Yes, I know, he says.
Hold your peace. Then Jericho: the same request, the same oath, another band of prophets, the same answer. Then the Jordan.
Elisha will not be sent away.

teach.b: At the Jordan, Elijah rolls up his mantle, his rough prophet's cloak, and strikes the water. The river divides, and they cross on dry ground. Elijah turns: ask what I shall do for thee, before I am taken.
And Elisha asks: "let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me."

In Israel's inheritance law, the firstborn son received a double share, so some readers hear Elisha asking to be the heir. Some Jewish commentators also read it more literally, as twice his teacher's wonders.
Elijah answers honestly: thou hast asked a hard thing. If you see me when I'm taken, it will be so; if not, it won't.

As they walk and talk, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separate them, and Elijah goes up by a whirlwind into heaven. Elisha cries out: my father, my father, the chariot of Israel and the horsemen thereof.
He tears his clothes in two. Grief first. Then he picks up the mantle that fell from Elijah, walks back to the Jordan, strikes the water with it and asks, where is the Lord, the God of Elijah?

teach.h: A DOUBLE PORTION OF THY SPIRIT.
teach.b: The prophets watching from Jericho say: the spirit of Elijah rests on Elisha. The inheritance doesn't arrive as a feeling.
It arrives as an old cloak lying on the ground, and a river that still has to be crossed.
And in Jewish tradition Elijah never quite leaves the story: tradition says he will return to announce redemption, and a cup is poured for him at the Passover seder.

how: Jews remember Elijah at the Passover seder with a cup poured for him, and the song Eliyahu HaNavi, asking for his return, is sung at the end of Shabbat.

o: a cloak handed down from a dying father
a double portion: the firstborn heir's share
a single blessing spoken over a student

games.q: a double portion — tap the pairs.
p: strikes the Jordan, and it divides

s: Elijah granted the double portion on the spot
he called it a hard thing: only if Elisha saw him taken would it be so.
Elisha struck the Jordan with Elijah's mantle
he asked, where is the Lord, the God of Elijah? and the water divided.
Elisha left Elijah at Beth-el as he was told
each time he answered, I will not leave thee.

games.q: you're Elisha. your teacher asks what he can do for you before he's taken. what do you ask for?
o: that he stay a little longer.
a double portion of his spirit.
games.why: Elisha asks for a double portion of his spirit. Elijah says it's a hard thing: if you see me taken, it will be so.

practice: Recall someone who taught you, cared for you, or started something good and then moved on, or passed on, and name one piece of what they did that you admired: a way of welcoming people, a recipe.
That's the mantle on the ground; picture picking it up. If you pray, you can remember them by name.

wordCard.voice: Pi shnayim. The Hebrew for a double portion, the share Elisha asked for as his teacher was taken. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: pi shnayim, a double portion, in 2 Kings 2:9.

carryVoice: Your line: an old cloak lying on the ground. What a teacher leaves still has to be picked up. Day seven hundred seventy-one.

sources.q: let a double portion of thy spirit be upon me
